name: Oxabolone
summary: An obscure nandrolone-family anabolic steroid that was never marketed itself and is banned in sport, with almost no published research.
lead: Oxabolone (also called 4-hydroxy-19-nortestosterone) is a synthetic anabolic-androgenic steroid in the nandrolone (19-nortestosterone) group. The parent compound was never marketed as a drug; its cipionate ester, oxabolone cipionate, is the form that has seen medical use, given by intramuscular injection.

name: SM-130686
summary: An experimental oral oxindole growth hormone secretagogue known from lab and animal papers, with no human trials of muscle or appearance effects.
lead: SM-130686 is an experimental, orally active, non-peptide growth hormone secretagogue built on an oxindole scaffold. It was characterised in the early 2000s as a ghrelin receptor agonist that stimulates growth hormone release.

name: Bezafibrate
summary: A prescription fibrate and pan-PPAR agonist for blood lipids, discussed in fat-loss circles only by association with PPAR-delta compounds.
lead: Bezafibrate is an oral fibrate lipid-lowering drug sold under brand names such as Bezalip. It lowers LDL cholesterol and triglycerides and raises HDL cholesterol, and it is described as a pan-agonist of the peroxisome proliferator-activated receptors (PPARs), acting on alpha, gamma and delta subtypes.

name: Seladelpar
summary: An FDA-approved PPAR-delta agonist for primary biliary cholangitis; its fat-loss relevance comes only from sharing a target with GW501516.
lead: Seladelpar (brand name Livdelzi; research codes MBX-8025 and RWJ-800025) is an oral, selective peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor delta (PPAR-delta) agonist. The US FDA approved it in August 2024 for primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), together with ursodeoxycholic acid in adults with an inadequate response to it, or alone in those who cannot tolerate it.

name: Elafibranor
summary: An approved dual PPAR-alpha/delta agonist for primary biliary cholangitis, with no research on appearance or fat-loss outcomes.
lead: Elafibranor (brand name Iqirvo; also GFT505) is an oral dual PPAR-alpha and PPAR-delta agonist developed by Genfit and marketed by Ipsen for primary biliary cholangitis (PBC). The US FDA granted accelerated approval in June 2024, and the EU granted conditional authorization in September 2024.

name: GW0742
summary: A GSK PPAR-delta research compound sold gray-market as "Cardarine 2.0", with lab and animal data only and no human trials.
lead: GW0742 (also GW610742 and proposed trade name fitorine) is an investigational PPAR-delta (PPAR-beta/delta) agonist investigated by GlaxoSmithKline and used widely as a laboratory tool compound. It is not an approved medicine.

name: L-165041
summary: A lab PPAR-delta agonist used in cell and mouse studies; no human fat-loss data exist.
lead: L-165041 is a research chemical that selectively activates PPAR-delta (PPARbeta/delta), a nuclear receptor involved in the regulation of fatty acid metabolism. It is used in laboratory studies of lipid metabolism, heart, blood vessel and nerve cell biology, and is listed by chemical suppliers as a research tool.

name: Acadesine
summary: AMPK activator hyped as an exercise mimetic; no human fat-loss evidence, and banned in sport.
lead: Acadesine, also called AICAR or AICA riboside, is a nucleoside that activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), an enzyme that senses cellular energy status. It was studied clinically for protecting the heart during surgery and in some blood cancers, and in 2008 a mouse study described it as an exercise mimetic, which led to interest from athletes and in online fat-loss and performance discussions.

name: SLU-PP-332
summary: Mouse-tested ERR agonist billed as an exercise mimetic; no human data exist.
lead: SLU-PP-332 is an experimental synthetic agonist of the estrogen-related receptors (ERR alpha, beta and gamma), described by its developers as an exercise mimetic because it triggered an exercise-like gene program and increased running capacity in mice.

name: BAM-15
summary: A mitochondrial uncoupler that burns fat in mice and is traded online as a 'safer DNP'; no human data exist.
lead: BAM15 is an experimental mitochondrial uncoupler, a small molecule that lets protons leak across the inner mitochondrial membrane so that nutrient oxidation produces heat rather than ATP. It was identified in a 2014 screen as an uncoupler that did not depolarize the plasma membrane.

name: Adipotide
summary: Experimental fat-vessel-targeting peptide that cut weight in monkeys; no human data and development stopped.
lead: Adipotide (also called prohibitin-targeting peptide 1, FTPP or TP01) is an experimental peptidomimetic designed to bind prohibitin and annexin A2 on the blood vessels feeding white fat, inducing the death of those vessels and, in turn, fat tissue.

name: Fenfluramine
summary: Former prescription diet drug withdrawn in 1997 over heart valve harm; now a restricted epilepsy medicine.
lead: Fenfluramine is an amphetamine-derived serotonin-releasing drug. Introduced in France in 1963 and approved in the United States in 1973 as an appetite suppressant (brand name Pondimin), it was widely used for weight loss, often with phentermine in the combination known as fen-phen.

name: Ephedrine/caffeine (ECA stack)
summary: A classic ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin cutting stack with modest reported fat-loss effects and a long regulatory history.
lead: The ECA stack is a combination of ephedrine, caffeine and aspirin used as a fat-loss and energy aid, particularly in bodybuilding and physique-cutting circles. Ephedrine is a sympathomimetic stimulant derived from or chemically identical to the alkaloids of the ephedra plant, and caffeine is thought to amplify its effects.
claims: ECA raises metabolism and suppresses appetite for fat loss
It is only worthwhile alongside exercise
It is safe if you have no heart problems

name: Zenagamtide
summary: Novo Nordisk's investigational GLP-1 plus amylin dual agonist, with large weight-loss figures in early trials and no approval yet.
lead: Zenagamtide, better known by the name amycretin, is an investigational once-weekly injectable and daily oral drug from Novo Nordisk that activates both the GLP-1 and amylin receptors within a single peptide molecule. It is being developed for obesity and type 2 diabetes and is not approved.

name: Enicepatide
summary: Roche's weekly GLP-1/GIP dual agonist, now in phase 3 and headed for a tirzepatide head-to-head.
lead: Enicepatide (CT-388, RO7795068) is an investigational once-weekly injectable drug that activates the GLP-1 and GIP receptors, developed by Roche for obesity and type 2 diabetes. It is described as signal-biased, meaning it shows minimal beta-arrestin coupling at either receptor.

name: CT-996
summary: Roche's experimental oral GLP-1 pill, with registered phase 2 trials and no results seen yet.
lead: CT-996 is an investigational oral small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist from Roche, also registered under the code RO7795081 and the name tifeglipron. Small-molecule oral GLP-1 agonists are a class designed to avoid the injection requirement of peptide drugs.

name: Petrelintide
summary: A weekly amylin-analogue obesity drug from Zealand and Roche, now in phase 3.
lead: Petrelintide (ZP8396) is an investigational once-weekly amylin analogue discovered by Zealand Pharma for weight management. In March 2025 Roche entered a collaboration with Zealand to co-develop and co-commercialise it, alone and in combination with CT-388 (enicepatide).

name: Eloralintide
summary: Lilly's weekly amylin agonist, with reported weight loss of roughly 9 to 20 percent at 48 weeks in phase 2.
lead: Eloralintide (LY3841136) is an investigational once-weekly selective amylin receptor agonist from Eli Lilly for obesity. It is not approved.

name: Maridebart cafraglutide
summary: Amgen's monthly GLP-1 agonist / GIP-blocker injection, still in phase 3, with roughly 12-16% weight loss at a year in phase 2.
lead: Maridebart cafraglutide, also known as MariTide and formerly AMG 133, is an investigational drug developed by Amgen for obesity and related conditions. It is a long-acting antibody-peptide conjugate: a fully human antibody that blocks the GIP receptor, linked to GLP-1 analogue peptides that activate the GLP-1 receptor.

name: Aleniglipron
summary: An experimental once-daily GLP-1 pill that cut weight by about 8-11% (placebo-adjusted) over 36 weeks in phase 2b.
lead: Aleniglipron (development code GSBR-1290) is an investigational oral, small-molecule glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonist being developed for obesity and overweight. Unlike injectable peptide GLP-1 drugs such as semaglutide, it is a non-peptide pill taken once daily.

name: ACCG-2671
summary: An early-stage oral amylin agonist for obesity known only from a single first-in-human trial registration.
lead: ACCG-2671 is an investigational oral small-molecule amylin receptor agonist being studied for obesity. The only public record of it is a registered first-in-human phase 1/2 trial examining its safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics and the effect of food.

name: Elecoglipron
summary: AstraZeneca's once-daily oral GLP-1 pill, with up to about 10% weight loss at 26 weeks in phase 2 and phase 3 now under way.
lead: Elecoglipron (AZD5004, also ECC5004) is an investigational oral, small-molecule GLP-1 receptor agonist developed by AstraZeneca for weight management and type 2 diabetes. It is taken as a once-daily tablet without food or fluid restrictions.

name: AZD6234
summary: AstraZeneca's weekly-style amylin agonist injection for obesity, with phase 3 registered but no published efficacy results.
lead: AZD6234 is an investigational long-acting selective amylin receptor agonist developed by AstraZeneca for obesity and type 2 diabetes, given by subcutaneous injection.

name: AZD9550
summary: AstraZeneca's experimental GLP-1/glucagon injection, tested alone and with an amylin agonist, with no published results yet.
lead: AZD9550 is an investigational GLP-1/glucagon receptor dual agonist from AstraZeneca, given by subcutaneous injection and studied for obesity and related liver disease.

name: Berobenatide
summary: Pfizer's investigational monthly GLP-1 agonist for obesity; only Phase 3 registrations exist so far.
lead: Berobenatide (also written PF-08653944 and MET-097i) is an investigational long-acting GLP-1 receptor agonist being developed by Pfizer for weight management. It is not approved anywhere and has no appearance-related indication. Information available publicly is limited to clinical trial registrations.

name: PF-08653945
summary: Pfizer's early-stage amylin analogue for obesity; nothing published on it yet.
lead: PF-08653945 (also MET-233i) is an investigational amylin analogue for weight management, listed as being developed by Pfizer. It is not approved and has no published human trial results in the sources reviewed.

name: ABBV-295
summary: AbbVie's injectable amylin analogue for obesity, now in early trials with no results out.
lead: ABBV-295 (also GUB014295) is an investigational amylin analogue given by subcutaneous injection, being developed by AbbVie for obesity. It is not approved.

name: Pramlintide
summary: Approved amylin analogue for insulin-treated diabetes; weight loss is a side-effect signal, not an approved use.
lead: Pramlintide (brand name Symlin) is a synthetic analogue of amylin, a hormone released by pancreatic beta cells with insulin. The US FDA approved it in March 2005 as an add-on to mealtime insulin in people with type 1 or type 2 diabetes who have not reached glucose targets. It is injected subcutaneously.

name: Dulaglutide
summary: Weekly GLP-1 diabetes drug with proven cardiovascular benefit and modest weight loss; not approved for obesity.
lead: Dulaglutide (brand name Trulicity) is a once-weekly injectable GLP-1 receptor agonist made by Eli Lilly for type 2 diabetes. It consists of GLP-1 linked to a fragment of human IgG4 antibody, extending its duration of action. The FDA approved it in September 2014 and the EU in November 2014.

name: Lixisenatide
summary: Short-acting daily GLP-1 diabetes drug, cardiovascular-neutral in ELIXA; minor role in weight loss.
lead: Lixisenatide (Lyxumia in the EU, Adlyxin in the US) is a once-daily injectable short-acting GLP-1 receptor agonist for type 2 diabetes, developed by Zealand Pharma and licensed to Sanofi in 2003. It was approved in the EU in February 2013 and in the US in July 2016.
